To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serum CXCL9 and 11 are significantly increased in patients with mixed cryoglobulinemia and hepatitis C, in presence or absence of autoimmune thyroiditis, compared to healthy controls.

1) serum CXCL9 and 2) CXCL11 are significantly increased in MC+HVC patients with or without AT, and 3) serum CXCL11 and 4) CXCL9 levels are significantly related in MC+HUV patients with or without autoimmune thyroiditis.

serum CXCL9 and its receptor CXCL11 are markedly increased in patients with mixed cryoglobulinemia (MC) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection compared to healthy subjects, and that their levels are further increased in the presence of autoimmune thyroiditis, a common comorbidity of MC+HCV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the first demonstration that in MC+HVC patients, CXCL9 and especially CXCL11 serum levels are markedly increased, in presence or absence of AT.
the role of CXCL9, and CXCL11 chemokines in MC+HVC and in MC+HVEC with AT.
the role of CXCL9, CXCL11, and their relation in the pathogenesis of MC+HCV, with or without AT.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

CXCL9 and, to a lesser extent, CXCL11 are significantly increased in MC+HVC patients with or without AT and this is the first evidence of a possible role of these two chemokines as markers of MC+HCV and/or AT.

the serum CXCL9 and 11 levels in MC+HVC patients, in presence or absence of AT, are significantly higher than in healthy controls, and that in MC+HCCV patients increased levels of CXCL11 are significantly associated with the concomitant presence of AT.
CXCL9 and 11 are significantly up-regulated in MC+HVC, and this is more pronounced when thyroiditis is associated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in MC+HVC patients, in presence or absence of AT, serum levels of CXCR3 ligands (CXCL9 and CXLC11) are markedly increased.
CXCL9 and/or CXCL11 serum levels could be considered as a marker for MC+HCV, and in particular, for MC+HVC patients affected by AT.
CXCL9 and 11 may be involved in the pathogenesis of MC+HCV in the presence/absence AT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CXCL9 and/or CXCL11 may represent potential biomarkers in MC+HVC and may be useful for monitoring disease activity.

serum CXCL9 and/or CXCL11 could be used as a diagnostic marker in patients with MC, especially in those with concomitant AT, in whom the presence of these chemokines may be considered as a marker of a more severe clinical picture and of a higher risk of developing other autoimmune diseases.
CXCL9 and, especially, CXCL11 could represent a useful marker for the identification of MC+HCV in presence of AT, and could be involved in the development of AT.
